objections.title: The “heirloom” objection: helium and sponge cake
objections.objection: PPC pictures causation as passing heirlooms down the line: the cause has a property and hands it to the effect. But nature is full of novelty. Helium has properties the hydrogen it came from lacked. A sponge cake is spongy, yet none of its ingredients — eggs, flour, butter — is spongy. So effects routinely contain what their causes lacked, and PPC is false.
objections.reply:
Feser makes two points here (the third, on triviality, is the next objection).

1. **Wrong target: material cause vs. total cause.** By Cottingham’s own admission, the examples look only at the *materials*. PPC says the effect’s features are in its **total** cause — the materials plus agents, powers, processes, and conditions (for the cake: the baker, the mixing, the oven’s heat). Restricting PPC to ingredients and then refuting that restricted version is a straw man.
2. **Wrong mode: formal presence isn’t required.** The heirloom reading assumes the feature must be in the cause *formally*. Defenders of PPC explicitly deny this. As one Thomist put it, a boy needn’t have a black eye to give one; as Aquinas put it, a hot body doesn’t transfer its own numerically identical heat but, by its power, actualizes a new heat that was potential in the thing heated. The effect’s features can be in the total cause **virtually** or **eminently**.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Then PPC just means the cause had the power to produce the effect — isn’t that obvious?” — agree that it is close to obvious once stated correctly. That is its strength, not its weakness. The work it does in natural theology comes from applying an obvious principle to the question of what could produce *existence itself*, intellect, and so on. If they press that emergent properties are genuinely “new,” point out that novelty of *instance* (a new heat, a new sponginess) is not the same as something from nothing: the total cause had the power to produce it, which is all PPC claims.

objections.title: “Potentially present” makes PPC trivial
objections.objection: Grant that sponginess doesn’t come from nothing — it emerges from the chemistry of mixing and baking. That still doesn’t show it was “present” in the materials. And if the defender says it was there *potentially*, PPC is rescued only by being made trivially true: of course whatever happens was possible beforehand.
objections.reply:
1. Feser happily accepts the language of potentiality. As the Aquinas passage says, the characteristics that end up in the effect were in it potentially, and in the $20 example the virtual and eminent cases involve real potentialities — the account’s capacity to be drawn on, the press’s capacity to print.
2. But appealing to potentialities is not trivial. Such explanations may be only *minimally* informative, but minimal information is still information. Saying your $20 came from my bank account’s power to be drawn on genuinely explains something.
3. The proof that PPC isn’t vacuous: naturalists use it to reach substantive conclusions. Churchland argues that because humans arise from wholly material causes by wholly material processes, humans are wholly material — an inference that assumes a wholly material total cause can only yield a wholly material effect. Dualists accept the same principle and argue in reverse from the immateriality of intellect. A trivial principle couldn’t settle anything, yet both sides treat this one as decisive.
objections.pushback: If they say, “The Churchland point shows only that some philosophers use it, not that it’s true,” reply that the question here was whether it is *trivial*, and a principle that carries real argumentative weight for both materialists and dualists is not. Its truth rests on PC and PSR: a feature of an effect not accounted for by anything in its total cause would be an actualization with no actualizer and a fact with no explanation.

objections.title: Evolution gets more from less
objections.objection: Evolution shows that simpler life forms give rise to more complex ones. The complex effect contains more than the simple cause — a straightforward counterexample to the claim that the effect can’t exceed its cause.
objections.reply:
1. Even on the standard naturalistic account (not just theistic versions), a simpler organism doesn’t produce a more complex one all by itself. Every species is a variation on genetic material that has existed since life began.
2. New variations arise when existing genetic material, a mutation (from a replication copying error, or from radiation or chemical damage), and environmental circumstances combine, so that the trait is advantageous in that setting. None of these factors alone would suffice; together they are the total cause.
3. So evolution *respects* PPC: the new variation’s features are present, in some way, in the combined factors.
4. Feser adds Paul Davies’ point: to deny that a new life form’s information comes from some combination of prior factors — including the environment, not only inheritance — would conflict with the second law of thermodynamics, according to which order and information tend to decrease in a closed system.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But the overall trend is from simple to complex,” reply that PPC is about the *total* cause at each step, and the naturalistic account itself insists the environment and physical processes supply what the genome alone lacks. If they go further and say information can simply appear from nothing, they are now contradicting both PSR and (per Davies) thermodynamics — a heavier cost than accepting PPC.

objections.title: “These are medieval relics no modern philosopher accepts”
objections.objection: Proportionate causality and “action follows being” are Scholastic slogans. Modern philosophy moved past them, and you can’t build an account of God on discarded medieval metaphysics.
objections.reply:
1. Both principles follow from PSR and PC, which earlier chapters defended at length; they stand or fall on their merits, not on their age.
2. Contemporary naturalists implicitly rely on them. Churchland’s argument for materialism assumes PPC.
3. Searle’s criticism of property dualism relies on *agere sequitur esse*: if a mental property is really over and above the brain, it can’t be a property of the brain and must be a separate entity; if it is a property of the brain, it can’t be over and above it. Others find it mysterious how a wholly material brain could yield immaterial properties — the same principle again.
4. Even a materialist who rejects Aquinas’ premise that thought is immaterial can accept his conditional: *if* intellect is immaterial, its subject must be immaterial.

So what looks like a relic is something many secular philosophers are committed to.
objections.pushback: If they grant the naturalists use it but still say it could be false, ask for a clear case where an activity really outruns the nature of its subject with nothing else making it do so. Feser’s own qualification (the puppet moves only because the puppeteer moves it) shows that apparent exceptions involve an outside agent, which confirms the principle rather than refuting it.

objections.title: Deny actuality or deny potentiality (Heraclitus and Parmenides)
objections.objection: Feser’s argument that being is analogical needs both actuality and potentiality to be real. But a Parmenidean can deny potentiality (change is illusion), and a Heraclitean can deny actuality (there is only flux, nothing stable). Either way the argument collapses.
objections.reply:
1. **Against Parmenides**: denying potentiality means denying change, which chapter 1 showed can’t be done coherently (even the experience of thinking through an argument is a succession).
2. **Against Heraclitus**: pure flux is just as incoherent.
- There would be no persisting self, so the person who reaches the conclusion wouldn’t be the one who entertained the premises.
- There would be no single, stable argument to present to critics or repeat to oneself.
- Change is always change *toward* something: a melting ice cube moves toward liquidity and flatness — new actualities, however temporary.
- A thing changes in the ways it does because of what it actually is: the ice melts because it is water, not wood or glass.

So premises 1 and 2 cannot coherently be denied.
objections.pushback: If they suggest a softer view — “there are only events, no enduring things” — ask what makes a given event the kind of event it is and why it tends toward some outcomes rather than others. Any answer smuggles actuality back in. And for Parmenideans: the claim that change is an illusion needs the illusion itself to change (appear, then disappear), which is still change.

objections.title: Act and potency differ only in how we talk
objections.objection: Grant that we talk about what a thing actually is and what it could become. That is a distinction in our concepts or language, not in reality. So premise 3 — that potentiality is *really* distinct from actuality — is false, and the analogy of being loses its basis.
objections.reply:
1. We already have at least one real case: chapter 4 argued that essence and existence are really distinct in things and relate as potency to act.
2. More generally, if the distinction were merely conceptual — two ways of describing one and the same reality — then that single reality would be either an actuality (and potentiality would be unreal) or a potentiality (and actuality would be unreal). That would amount to denying premise 1 or premise 2, which we have seen can’t coherently be done.
3. Hence premise 3 stands, and with premises 4–6 (same sense would collapse the distinction; unrelated sense would make potency unreal; the three uses exhaust literal usage) the conclusion follows: potency has being in a sense analogous to act.
objections.pushback: If they say, “There’s just the actual thing, and ‘potential’ describes what it would do in various circumstances,” ask what grounds those truths. If nothing in the actual ice cube grounds its capacity to melt (which a lump of wood lacks), the difference between ice and wood becomes an inexplicable brute fact. If something does ground it, that something is not the same as the ice’s current solidity — which is the real distinction.

objections.title: God-talk is either anthropomorphic or empty
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; Humean-style critics; also strictly apophatic theologians from the other side
objections.objection: Either words like “exists,” “powerful,” and “good” mean the same when applied to God as to us — making God a big human — or they mean something entirely different, in which case we don’t know what we’re saying. So either theology is anthropomorphic, or it says nothing. The most one can honestly say is what God is not.
objections.reply:
1. Feser agrees that univocal predication can’t work. The proofs conclude to something purely actual, simple, immaterial, immutable, eternal; words formed for changeable material things can’t apply to it in the same sense.
2. But pure negative theology fails too. “God exists” and “God causes the world” are affirmative statements; if we could only deny things of God, we couldn’t even state the conclusions of the proofs. Negation is part of the story, not the whole of it.
3. Equivocation fails as well. If God’s “power” has nothing to do with power, what does it mean? Try completing “God has ‘power’ in the sense that he ___.” A univocal filler reintroduces anthropomorphism; an equivocal one just moves the mystery. The upshot would be agnosticism or even atheism — maybe not even meaningful speech.
4. The dilemma is false because there is a third, literal use of language — analogical predication by attribution and proper proportionality — which we already needed (for “being” said of act and potency) before any theology.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But you can’t tell me exactly what God’s knowledge is like,” agree: analogical concepts are applied indeterminately. But indeterminate is not empty. We know what we are affirming (a real perfection of which our knowledge is a limited likeness) and what we are denying (the limits and composition that go with it in us).

objections.title: Analogy is special pleading invented to save theology
objections.objection: The “analogy” doctrine looks like an ad hoc device: when theists can’t make sense of their claims literally, they declare their words analogical. We don’t need a special semantics anywhere else.
objections.reply:
1. The doctrine is **independently motivated**. Feser’s seven-step argument derives it from the act/potency distinction alone — which one could accept without ever accepting any argument for God.
2. Ordinary language is shot through with analogy that no one regards as special pleading: good wine and good people; healthy food and healthy people; seeing a tree and seeing a proof; life in plants and in animals.
3. Science does the same. Physics speaks of entities with both wave-like and particle-like properties and of space itself being curved, stretching common-sense concepts far beyond their home; this seems intelligible only analogically. We should expect at least as much stretching when describing the cause of there being a material world at all.
4. And analogical predication is literal: nonunivocal does not mean nonliteral.
objections.pushback: If they respond that physics can back its analogies with mathematics and experiment, reply that theology backs its analogies with demonstrative argument: the proofs tell us *which* features are removed (potency, composition, limitation) and *why* the perfection must be present (PPC). That is a disciplined constraint, not a blank check.

objections.title: The First Cause might have potency in its activity
objections.objection: Grant that the first cause’s *existence* involves no actualization — that’s what lets it stop the regress. Why couldn’t its *activity* still involve potentiality — say, its activity of actualizing other things? Then it would be uncaused in existence yet not purely actual, and the arguments for unity and the other attributes would fail.
objections.reply:
1. **Agere sequitur esse.** Action reflects being. If a thing exists in a purely actual way, how could its acting be less than purely actual? Existence is the most fundamental thing about a being; everything else follows from it. There is nothing in a purely actual nature from which potentialities for activity could arise.
2. **Composition.** Such a being would have parts — an actual part and a potential part. Chapter 2 showed that composites need a cause of the combining of their parts, and that cause must be extrinsic (an intrinsic one would cause itself). This holds even if the thing always existed: the need is for an *ontologically* prior cause, not a temporally prior one. But a first cause with a cause of its own isn’t first and can’t end the hierarchical regress.
3. So the First Cause is purely actual in activity as well as existence.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Why not just say God is uncaused and composite — a brute fact?” point out that this abandons the principle the proofs rest on (composites need causes) at the precise moment it becomes inconvenient, and it would leave us with a being that is ultimate only by stipulation. It would also undermine the arguments that got us to God in the first place.

objections.title: Why not two (or many) gods?
objections.whoRaises: Polytheist; skeptic probing the leap to monotheism
objections.objection: Even if there must be a purely actual cause, why only one? Perhaps there are several, each purely actual, distinguished in some way — or perhaps each proof reaches a different ultimate being.
objections.reply:
1. For there to be more than one thing of a kind, there must be a distinction between individual and species (as matter distinguishes two humans) or between species and genus (as rationality distinguishes humans within the genus animal).
2. Such distinctions require parts — genus plus difference, matter plus form — and parts entail potentiality: matter is potentially this or something else; a genus is potentially one species or another; parts only potentially compose a whole until actualized.
3. A purely actual being has no potency and hence no such parts, so it can’t be one member of a kind that could have others. It is unique in principle.
4. Nor can we distinguish two purely actual beings by other kinds of parts, such as substance and accidents: any composition brings potency.
5. And the five proofs don’t reach five beings: pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, and necessity each entail the others, so they all describe the same unique reality.
objections.pushback: If they propose that two gods might differ by a mere relation (e.g., by their positions), ask what in each god grounds the different relation. If nothing intrinsic differs, they’re not two; if something intrinsic differs, it is a part or a limitation, and that brings potency. Two purely actual beings would be indistinguishable in every intrinsic respect — which is just one being described twice.

objections.title: Theistic personalism: a personal God need not be simple
objections.whoRaises: “Theistic personalists” / “neo-theists” (Brian Davies’ and Norman Geisler’s labels): Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne, Charles Hartshorne and process theologians
objections.objection: Divine simplicity is a Greek philosophical import that makes God unintelligible. Better to think of God as a person like us — with distinct attributes of knowledge, power, goodness — only without our limitations: the unique member of the kind *person* at its maximum. Process theists add that, like any person, God changes in response to the world.
objections.reply:
1. The dispute isn’t about personhood. Classical theists attribute intellect and will to God and so regard him as personal. The issue is whether being personal puts God *in a genus* and makes him composite.
2. If God belonged to a kind, he would be unique only as a matter of contingent fact — like Zeus alone on Olympus or Odin alone in Asgard, whose natures would be unaltered. Monotheism would be a lucky accident.
3. If God had distinct parts or attributes, something would have to combine them, so he would need a cause and wouldn’t be the First Cause. Even if immaterial, he would be a superangel, and worshiping him would be idolatry.
4. Changeability (the process view) implies potency, and so composition.
5. Crucially, none of the five proofs supports such a being. Each concludes to a wholly noncomposite cause. So one cannot accept the proofs and reject simplicity; denying simplicity is implicitly atheism. That is why the tradition across paganism, Judaism, Islam, and Christianity — and the Catholic Church at Lateran IV and Vatican I, as well as Luther and Calvin — treated it as nonnegotiable.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But the God of Scripture seems to be a person who responds and changes,” note that this module deals with metaphysics; the classical tradition reads such language analogically, with Part B (ch6b) explaining how intellect, will, and love belong to God without composition. If they say simplicity makes God impersonal, point out that it is compatible with — indeed required for — God’s being the *source* of personal perfections, which he has eminently.

objections.title: Plantinga: simplicity makes God a single property — an abstract object
objections.whoRaises: Alvin Plantinga, Does God Have a Nature?
objections.objection: Simplicity says God is identical with each of his properties. Then each property is identical with every other, so God has just one property — flatly contrary to the obvious fact that he has several, such as power and mercy. Worse, if God is identical with a property, then God *is* a property, and properties are abstract objects. So God would be an abstract object, which is absurd for a being who knows and acts.
objections.reply:
Feser says Plantinga reads the doctrine through three assumptions of his own, each of which classical theists reject.

1. **Univocity.** Plantinga takes “wise” or “powerful” to mean the same of God and of Socrates. But predication of God is analogical: what we call power and knowledge in God is *analogous* to ours. That they are distinct in us doesn’t show they are distinct in him.
2. **Platonism about properties.** Plantinga treats properties as abstract objects in a third realm that things exemplify. For Aquinas, a thing’s essence, properties, and accidents are concrete constituents *of* the thing (Wolterstorff’s “constituent ontology”). So identifying God with his wisdom doesn’t identify him with an abstract object; no classical theist ever said God is a “property.”
3. **An overbroad notion of “property.”** Plantinga counts anything predicable as a property: being human, wise, barefoot, married to Xanthippe, Plato’s teacher, even being Socrates. Aquinas distinguishes the **essence** (rational animality), **properties** proper that flow from it (the capacity for amusement), **contingent accidents** (skin color), and mere **relations** (being Plato’s teacher). Lumping them together is what makes it sound as if simplicity would make God’s creating humans as essential to him as his wisdom.

The odd consequences come from these assumptions, not from simplicity. Plantinga also misreads analogy as nonliteral (it is literal) and misses the real stakes: not Platonic participation, but that a composite God would be caused and only contingently unique.
objections.pushback: If they ask, “So are God’s power and mercy the same thing or not?” answer: in God there is one simple reality; we form distinct concepts of it because we know it through distinct effects in creatures, and each concept truly (analogically) describes that one reality. The concepts are distinct; what they apply to in God isn’t divided. That no more makes the concepts synonyms than “morning star” and “evening star” are synonyms.

objections.title: Plantinga’s fallback: “call them characteristics”
objections.objection: Fine — Aquinas uses “property” more narrowly than I do. But that is merely verbal. Whatever we call them, God has many *characteristics* — power, mercy, being Creator — and simplicity still has to say they are all identical.
objections.reply:
1. This misses the point. Aquinas’ distinctions are not a semantic preference for using “property” in a restricted way.
2. They mark objective, extralinguistic metaphysical differences between a thing’s essence, its proper properties, its contingent accidents, its intrinsic accidents, and its relations to other things.
3. Once those differences are respected, simplicity only identifies God’s real, intrinsic perfections — not his relations to creatures (which are Cambridge properties; see Morris’s objection). The alleged implication that God’s contingent relations are identical with his essence never arises.
objections.pushback: If they insist that all true predications must correspond to some item in God, ask whether “Socrates is shorter than Plato” corresponds to an item in Socrates when only Plato has grown. It plainly doesn’t, and neither does “God is Creator” require a new item in God.

objections.title: Necessary and contingent properties can’t be identical
objections.whoRaises: Thomas Morris, Our Idea of God (see also Christopher Hughes)
objections.objection: Some things are true of God necessarily (he is omnipotent) and some only contingently (he created the world, though he needn’t have). The only good way to capture this is to say God has both necessary and contingent properties. But a necessary property can’t be identical to a contingent one. So not all God’s properties are identical, and simplicity is false.
objections.reply:
Setting aside the loose use of “property,” Feser follows Barry Miller, who builds on Peter Geach.

1. Distinguish **real** properties from mere **Cambridge** properties. Socrates growing hair is a real change; Socrates becoming shorter than Plato because Plato grew is a Cambridge change, giving Socrates only a Cambridge property.
2. Simplicity doesn’t deny that God has contingent properties of every sort — only contingent **real** ones. And it doesn’t say all God’s properties are identical — only his **real** ones.
3. Being Creator is a Cambridge property: it involves the world coming into existence, not a change in God.
4. So Morris is right that omnipotence (real, necessary) and having created the world (Cambridge, contingent) aren’t identical. But simplicity never implied they were.
objections.pushback: If they reply, “But creating is like Socrates *causing* Plato to grow, and that does change Socrates,” Feser’s answer (his footnote) is that this assumes the changes we undergo when acting must occur in any agent — a fallacy of accident. What is essential to causing is producing an effect in another, not changing oneself. If they then raise the modal-collapse worry, see that objection below.

objections.title: To act is to change
objections.whoRaises: Common objection to immutability (and Feser’s footnote on creation as Socrates-changing-Plato)
objections.objection: Acting always involves a change in the agent, not just in what it acts upon. When I type, the screen changes — but so do my fingers, my nervous system, and my thoughts. So if God creates, he changes, and an immutable God couldn’t create or do anything.
objections.reply:
1. It’s true that the agents we experience change in the course of acting. But inferring that every *possible* agent must do so commits the **fallacy of accident** — like reasoning that because every professor so far has been under nine feet tall, no possible professor could be taller. The link is contingent, not essential.
2. What is essential to acting, as Brian Davies points out, is bringing about an effect in another thing, not undergoing change oneself. Teaching essentially means causing someone to learn — not specifically lecturing or writing books. Creating essentially means causing the world to exist; nothing in that requires the Creator to change.
3. And God’s becoming Creator is a Cambridge change: the real change is in the world.
4. Immutability is also demanded independently: a purely actual being has no potency to actualize, and a simple being lacks the parts that real change (changing in one respect while staying the same in others) requires.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But I can’t imagine acting without changing,” agree — and note that imagination is tied to the material, changing agents we know. The question is whether *acting as such* entails change, and nothing in the concept of producing an effect does. We even have partial models: a magnet or the sun can produce effects without itself being altered in doing so (a course illustration; the analogy is imperfect since these things do change in other ways).

objections.title: An unchanging God can’t be alive
objections.objection: Living things grow, feed, move, and learn — life *is* change. A changeless God would be static, frozen, dead — more like a stone than a living being.
objections.reply:
1. This is another fallacy of accident: the living things we know change, but it doesn’t follow that every possible living thing must.
2. On the traditional Aristotelian account, what is essential to life is operating from an **internal principle** rather than being wholly moved by external forces (immanent rather than merely transient causation). An animal is alive because much of what it does flows from its own nature; a stone isn’t, because it does things (like breaking a window) only when something acts on it.
3. God acts without being acted upon by anything at all. Other living things are partly dependent — they must eat and breathe. So God has life in the fullest possible way.
4. The stone comparison gets it backward: the stone is the most dependent, God the least.
objections.pushback: If they say “life without change is inconceivable,” ask which is more alive: something that needs constant input from outside to keep functioning, or something whose activity is wholly from itself and lacks nothing. Change in creatures is a sign of their incompleteness — they change to acquire what they lack.

objections.title: Causing at t1 and at t2 means acting in time
objections.objection: Feser says God causes the existence of everything at every moment. Then God causes something to exist at t1, and causes something to exist at the later time t2. So he acts at t1 and again at t2 — which means he is in time.
objections.reply:
1. The inference is invalid. From *God causes it to be the case that X exists at t1* it doesn’t follow that *at t1, God causes X to exist* (a point Feser takes from Brian Davies). The temporal index belongs to the effect, not to the act.
2. God doesn’t perform a sequence of acts — creating at t1, conserving at t2, conserving again at t3. From outside time, in one act, he causes a temporal world in which X exists at t1, t2, t3, and so on.
3. Compare an author who conceives a whole story in a single flash of insight (an image Feser borrows from Stephen Barr): within the story, the middle follows the beginning; the author didn’t devise them one after the other.
objections.pushback: If they say “causing is always simultaneous with or prior to its effect, so it must be at a time,” reply that this generalizes from temporal causes (fallacy of accident again). If they say “then God can’t respond to prayers or events,” that belongs to Part B (knowledge and will), but in brief: God’s single timeless act includes the whole history, prayers and responses together, as the author’s single conception includes the plot’s every twist.

objections.title: The simultaneity argument: Socrates would be simultaneous with Obama
objections.objection: If God causes Socrates to exist in 469 B.C., Socrates’ existence must be simultaneous with God’s eternity; if God causes Obama to exist in A.D. 1961, Obama’s existence must be simultaneous with God’s eternity too. Simultaneity is transitive, so Socrates’ existence would be simultaneous with Obama’s. That is absurd, so timeless eternity is incoherent.
objections.reply:
1. The objection treats eternity as if it were a **point in time**, since only a point in time can be simultaneous with another point in time.
2. But the entire claim is that God does not exist at any point in time; he exists outside time altogether (Feser cites Davies and Paul Helm).
3. So the first two premises are false as stated: temporal events are not “simultaneous with” eternity in the ordinary, transitive sense of simultaneity.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Then what is the relation between God and a temporal event?” answer: causal dependence — the event exists because God causes it — not temporal location. A novel’s events all depend on the author’s one conception without being simultaneous with each other.

objections.title: Necessity is linguistic convention
objections.whoRaises: J. N. Findlay; Bertrand Russell (1948 BBC debate with Frederick Copleston)
objections.objection: Necessity belongs to statements, not to things. “All bachelors are unmarried” is necessary only because it is analytic — true in virtue of what the words mean — and it tells us about our linguistic conventions, not about the world. Extralinguistic reality can’t be necessary. God is supposed to be part of extralinguistic reality. So a “necessary being” is a confused notion.
objections.reply:
1. **Conventionalism is false on independent grounds.** It confuses **sentences** (linguistic items) with **propositions** (not linguistic). “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition, which would be true even if no language had ever existed. So the conventionality of sentences doesn’t make propositions — or their necessity — conventional.
2. That example is contingent, but truths of mathematics and logic (2 + 2 = 4; everything is identical to itself) are necessary, and it is notoriously hard to argue plausibly that they are conventions (chapter 3).
3. **The objection begs the question.** The proofs claim to show that there is an extralinguistic cause of the existence of things that exists necessarily, and they give an account of that necessity unrelated to convention: pure actuality, absolute simplicity, identity of essence and existence. Merely asserting that all necessity is linguistic presupposes the arguments are wrong without showing that they are.
objections.pushback: If they retreat to “at least necessity *de dicto* is all we understand,” ask whether they understand the claim that a thing whose essence is its existence can’t fail to exist. That is intelligible and not about words. If they say it’s still an ontological-argument trick, clarify: Feser isn’t deriving existence from a definition; the proofs establish God’s existence from the world first, and necessity follows from what that cause turns out to be.

objections.title: Schrader’s empty world
objections.whoRaises: David Schrader, “The Antinomy of Divine Necessity”
objections.objection: Imagine a world with nothing in it but a single green marble. Now imagine even the marble gone. You have imagined a world in which nothing exists — not even God. So there is a possible world without God, and God doesn’t exist necessarily.
objections.reply:
1. This works only if everything that exists or could exist — God included — is the kind of thing you can form a **mental image** of, present or absent. It isn’t (Feser cites Brian Leftow).
2. Compare: picture a universe containing only a chalkboard with “2 + 2 = 4” on it, then picture it erased. That shows nothing about whether 2 + 2 = 4 is necessary, because numbers aren’t imageable objects. You can picture numerals (“2,” “4,” or “II,” “IV”), but numerals are labels, not numbers.
3. What we can form an image of is simply irrelevant to what we can strictly conceive.
4. The same holds of God, who is wholly immaterial. You can’t picture God existing, let alone not existing. Mental imagery tells us nothing about God’s modal status, any more than it does about mathematics.
objections.pushback: If Schrader’s defender says, “I didn’t mean picture — I mean I can *conceive* a world with nothing,” move to the next objection’s reply: conceivability of worlds isn’t the right starting point for modal knowledge, and assuming God is absent from some conceivable world simply assumes he isn’t necessary.

objections.title: Conceivability of possible worlds is our guide to necessity
objections.whoRaises: Schrader, and much contemporary modal metaphysics
objections.objection: Even without mental images, we can coherently conceive a possible world containing nothing at all. Conceivability is our best guide to possibility. So it is possible that God not exist, and he is not a necessary being.
objections.reply:
1. From the Aristotelian-Thomistic point of view, this method gets things **backward**. We don’t first survey possible worlds and then read off what is possible or necessary for things.
2. Rather, we start with *actual* things, determine their essences, and from those draw conclusions about what is possible for them and necessarily true of them.
3. In God’s case the right procedure is: establish that God exists, determine his nature, and infer from that what is possible and necessary for him. That’s what the preceding chapters did: God is purely actual, absolutely simple, subsistent existence depending on nothing else — and so exists necessarily, and hence (if we use possible-worlds talk) in every possible world.
4. Schrader’s objection doesn’t show anything wrong with this reasoning; it simply assumes something is wrong with it, so it begs the question.
objections.pushback: If they say, “But surely an empty world is at least prima facie conceivable,” reply that apparent conceivability is defeasible: one can seem to conceive that some complex arithmetical claim is false until one works through the proof. Likewise, the ‘empty world’ seems conceivable only until one understands that a being whose essence is existence can’t fail to exist.

objections.title: “Who made God?”
objections.whoRaises: Popular skeptic (e.g., the “Who designed the designer?” line); not an objection Feser discusses in this section
objections.objection: If everything needs a cause, God needs one too. If God doesn’t need one, why does the universe? Positing God just pushes the question back a step.
objections.reply:
Using this module’s results (Feser takes up the objection directly in chapter 7):

1. The proofs never say *everything* needs a cause. They say that what has potentiality needing actualization, parts needing combination, an essence distinct from its existence, or contingent existence needs a cause.
2. This chapter shows that God has none of these features: he is purely actual, simple, subsistent existence, and necessary. He not only *needs* no cause; he *could not* have one (the eternity argument).
3. The universe, by contrast, is made of composite, changeable, contingent things. The asymmetry isn’t special pleading; it follows from a principled difference.
4. And if we suppose God had a cause, then the being we are talking about is not the First Cause, and the regress would continue to the being that is uncaused — which would then be God.
objections.pushback: If they say, “Then why not stop at the universe as the uncaused thing?” ask whether the universe (or its fundamental constituents) has parts, potentialities, or contingent existence. Everything physics tells us says it does — even fundamental particles have distinct attributes and come to be and pass away. So it can’t play the role of the First Cause.

objections.title: Modal collapse: if God is simple, isn’t everything necessary?
objections.whoRaises: Contemporary critics of divine simplicity (e.g., R. T. Mullins); not raised in this chapter
objections.objection: If God is simple, his act of creating is identical with his necessary essence. Then creating is as necessary as God’s existence, and the world exists necessarily — God couldn’t have refrained from creating. That contradicts both freedom and the contingency of the world.
objections.reply:
This chapter doesn’t address the objection by name, but it supplies the key tools; the fuller answer, involving divine will and freedom, belongs to Part B (ch6b).

1. Simplicity identifies God’s **real** perfections with his essence. Being Creator is a **Cambridge** property: the difference between a world where God creates and one where he doesn’t is a difference in the *world*, not an extra real feature in God (Geach/Miller, via Feser).
2. So the objection’s premise — that God’s creating is an intrinsic element of God identical with his essence — is exactly what the classical theist denies. What is identical with God’s essence is his one act of being, knowing, and willing; that this act has *this* world as a term is a contingent truth grounded in the world’s dependence on God.
3. By the same reasoning Feser uses for timeless causing: “God causes X” reports a relation of dependence in X, not a new real item in God.
objections.pushback: If they press, “But then what explains why God’s one act has this world as its term rather than none?” acknowledge that this is where the harder questions about divine freedom begin, and point to Feser’s treatment of will and freedom in ch6b. Note that this is a live contemporary debate among theists; honesty about that strengthens rather than weakens your case.

misconceptions.myth: PPC says a cause must literally resemble or contain its effect, so a creator of material things must be material.
misconceptions.correction: PPC allows an effect’s features to be in the cause formally, virtually, or eminently. God contains creaturely perfections eminently — as the one with power over the printing press “has” $20 bills without having any in his wallet.

misconceptions.myth: Calling God-talk “analogical” means it is metaphorical, poetic, or not literally true.
misconceptions.correction: Analogies of attribution and proper proportionality are literal uses of language. Only improper (metaphorical) proportionality is figurative. Nonunivocal does not mean nonliteral: God really exists and really knows, in ways analogous to ours.

misconceptions.myth: Divine simplicity means God has only one attribute and all our words for him are synonyms.
misconceptions.correction: Our concepts of God’s power, knowledge, and goodness are distinct, because we know them through distinct effects; each truly applies to the one undivided divine reality. Simplicity concerns what is in God, not the number of concepts we use.

misconceptions.myth: Simplicity makes God an abstract object, like a Platonic property.
misconceptions.correction: That follows only if one assumes, with Plantinga, that properties are abstract Platonic entities. For Aquinas, a thing’s essence and attributes are concrete constituents of it; and God is not a “property” at all but subsistent existence itself.

misconceptions.myth: Classical theists deny that God is personal; theistic personalists affirm it.
misconceptions.correction: Both ascribe intellect and will to God. The disagreement is whether being personal puts God in a genus alongside humans and angels and makes him composite. Classical theists say no.

misconceptions.myth: An immutable God is inert, frozen, or lifeless, and cannot act.
misconceptions.correction: Acting essentially is producing an effect, and living essentially is acting from an internal principle; neither requires change. God, wholly unacted upon, is maximally active and has life in the fullest sense.

misconceptions.myth: God’s eternity means he has existed for an infinitely long time and will go on forever.
misconceptions.correction: That is mere everlastingness. Feser argues that God is strictly timeless: no succession, no temporal stages, no moments added. Eternity is not a point or stretch of time.

misconceptions.myth: If God becomes Creator, something in God must have changed.
misconceptions.correction: Becoming Creator is a Cambridge change, like Socrates becoming shorter than Plato when only Plato grew. The real change is the world coming to be.

misconceptions.myth: Each of the five proofs reaches a different ultimate being, and one needs a sixth argument to show there is only one.
misconceptions.correction: The attributes established — pure actuality, simplicity, subsistent existence, necessity — entail one another, and pure actuality entails uniqueness. The five proofs are five routes to one God.

misconceptions.myth: Divine necessity means God’s existence follows from the definition of the word “God.”
misconceptions.correction: Feser does not use an ontological argument. The proofs first establish from the world that a First Cause exists; its necessity follows from its nature (pure actuality, simplicity, essence identical to existence), which is a real, extralinguistic feature.
